UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
LS Power Grid New York Corporation I 
New York Independent System Operator, Inc. 
)

DIRECT TESTIMONY OF PATRICK HAYES 
ON BEHALF OF 
LS POWER GRID NEW YORK CORPORATION I 
Large Load Network Upgrade Cost Recovery 
November 2026

EXHIBITS TO 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF PATRICK HAYES 
 
Exhibit No. 
Description

Illustrative MTRC Calculation

1 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF PATRICK HAYES 
I. INTRODUCTION AND EXPERIENCE 
1 
Q. 
PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS. 
2 
A. 
My name is Patrick Hayes. My business address is 16150 Main Circle Drive, Suite 310, 
3 
Chesterfield, Missouri 63017. 
4 
Q. 
BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED, AND WHAT ARE YOUR 
5 
RESPONSIBILITIES? 
6 
A. 
I am employed by LS Power and serve as Associate Vice President, Transmission 
7 
Regulatory. I lead regulatory strategy for LS Power’s transmission business across the 
8 
California Independent System Operator, Midcontinent Independent System Operator, PJM 
9 
Interconnection, New York Independent System Operator, and other regional markets. My 
10 
responsibilities include FERC policy, regional transmission planning, competitive 
11 
transmission development, cost allocation and recovery, tariff development, and large-load 
12 
interconnection. 
13 
Q. 
PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE AND 
14 
EDUCATION. 
15 
A. 
I previously served as LS Power’s Director of Transmission Business Development and 
16 
Manager of Transmission Policy. Earlier in my career, I held transmission policy, energy 
17 
trading, and asset optimization positions with Ameren. My experience includes developing 
18 
strategies for competitive transmission projects and utility partnerships, negotiating 
19 
commercial and ownership arrangements, evaluating transmission investments, and 
20 
coordinating multidisciplinary teams. I received a Bachelor of Science in Accounting from 
21 
the University of Missouri. 
22

2 
Q. 
ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU SUBMITTING THIS TESTIMONY? 
1 
A. 
I am testifying on behalf of LS Power Grid New York Corporation I (“LSPGNY”), a non-
2 
incumbent Transmission Owner in the New York Independent System Operator, Inc. 
3 
(“NYISO”) region. LSPGNY and the New York Power Authority developed Segment A of 
4 
the AC Transmission Public Policy Transmission Need, a 345 kV project between the 
5 
Marcy/Edic and New Scotland substations now in service as part of Central East Energy 
6 
Connect. 
7 
II. PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF TESTIMONY 
8 
Q. 
WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY? 
9 
A. 
I explain how LSPGNY proposes to recover the costs of Large Load-Driven Upgrades on 
10 
its facilities and protect other transmission customers from bearing costs caused by a large 
11 
load. LSPGNY would calculate upgrade revenue requirements under its formula rate and 
12 
recover the resulting amounts through NYISO under revised Rate Schedule 10. The 
13 
revenue requirements for Large Load-Driven Upgrades would be combined with Segment 
14 
A’s revenue requirement in a single Regulated Transmission Facilities Charge (“RTFC”), 
15 
using Segment A’s existing cost allocation. For upgrades covered by this filing, where 
16 
LSPGNY is the Connecting Transmission Owner, a Cost Recovery Agreement (“CRA”) 
17 
establishes the responsible Eligible Customer’s minimum revenue contribution and security 
18 
obligations. Projected Supplemental Minimum Transmission Revenue Contribution 
19 
(“Supplemental MTRC”) and Annual Termination Fee Remittances would be recognized as 
20 
general revenue credits in the Annual Projection. In the Annual Update, those projected 
21 
credits would be replaced by actual cash receipts, including applicable Security proceeds 
22 
received and applied to Supplemental MTRC obligations and Annual Termination Fee 
23

3 
Remittances received, under the formula rate template. Segment A’s existing tariff cost 
1 
allocation would apply to the combined RTFC, including the Large Load-Driven Upgrade 
2 
costs and applicable CRA revenue credits. 
3 
I describe the Commission’s Show Cause Order, LSPGNY’s stakeholder outreach, the 
4 
proposed CRA, and the tariff and protocol changes needed to implement it. My testimony 
5 
addresses policy and implementation. The detailed formula-rate calculations and supporting 
6 
workpapers are addressed in the separate rate testimony of Eric Arzola. 
7 
Q.  ARE YOU SPONSORING ANY EXHIBITS IN SUPPORT OF YOUR TESTIMONY 
8 
IN THIS CASE? 
9 
A.  Yes. I am sponsoring the following exhibits: 
10 
Exhibit No. 
Description 
GNY-101: 
Illustrative MTRC Calculation 
GNY-102: 
Example Reconciliation Statement 
GNY-103: 
Example Charge Statement 
III. THE NYISO SHOW CAUSE ORDER 
11 
Q. 
WHAT DID THE COMMISSION DIRECT IN THIS PROCEEDING? 
12 
A. 
On June 18, 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”) 
13 
instituted this proceeding under section 206 of the Federal Power Act. It directed NYISO 
14 
and the named Transmission Owners, including LSPGNY, to show cause why the NYISO 
15 
Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”) remains just and reasonable and free of undue 
16 
discrimination or preference without provisions addressing the Commission’s concerns, or 
17 
to explain what tariff changes would remedy them if the Commission establishes a 
18 
replacement rate. The Commission granted a 90-day abeyance on August 14, 2026, setting 
19 
November 16, 2026, as the response deadline, subject to the order’s provision for a 
20

4 
respondent that makes a timely section 205 filing addressing the preliminary findings. See 
1 
N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,216 at P 3 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”); 
2 
Order Granting Abeyance, Docket No. EL26-69-000, at PP 10–11 (Aug. 14, 2026). 
3 
Q. 
WHICH ASPECTS OF THE SHOW CAUSE ORDER DOES YOUR TESTIMONY 
4 
ADDRESS? 
5 
A. 
I address the Commission’s preliminary findings on cost transparency and cost shifting. 
6 
The Commission identified a risk that other transmission customers could pay for upgrades 
7 
built for a large load if that load is delayed, takes less service than requested, or never 
8 
materializes. It identified public posting of upgrade and cost information and a pro forma 
9 
CRA between the relevant Transmission Owner and the Eligible Customer as potential 
10 
remedies. The Commission linked the minimum contribution to the requested megawatts 
11 
that drive the need for upgrades, sought sufficient credit support, and expected amounts 
12 
paid under a CRA to be credited appropriately to the Transmission Owner’s revenue 
13 
requirement. It also contemplated a separate workpaper in the annual formula-rate 
14 
informational filing. See Show Cause Order at PP 72–82, 83–91. 
15 
Q. 
WHY DO THOSE FINDINGS RAISE A DISTINCT ISSUE FOR LSPGNY? 
16 
A. 
LSPGNY is a Transmission Owner for purposes of the NYISO tariffs under its Operating 
17 
Agreement with NYISO. It has no franchised retail service territory or obligation to serve 
18 
retail load and has no Transmission Service Charge (“TSC”) under Attachment H. Its 
19 
Commission-accepted formula rate is part of Rate Schedule 10, which provides for 
20 
recovery of eligible projects under Attachment Y. Segment A is such a project. The 
21 
existing eligibility provisions do not expressly cover Network Upgrades identified to serve 
22 
a large load through the load interconnection process. Rate Schedule 10 also excludes 
23

5 
projects undertaken through the Local Transmission Owner Planning Process. See NYISO 
1 
Service Agreement No. 2627, Operating Agreement § 1.01, Docket No. ER21-2104-000; 
2 
NYISO OATT §§ 6.10.1, 6.10.7, 14.1, and 31.5.1.5. 
3 
A large load can require an upgrade to an LSPGNY facility even when it connects to 
4 
another Transmission Owner’s system. A study or interconnection agreement can identify 
5 
the facilities and assign cost responsibility. LSPGNY also needs a tariff provision that 
6 
authorizes recovery of the associated cost of service and specifies how NYISO will bill the 
7 
responsible customer and credit CRA payments. That recovery mechanism is needed 
8 
whether LSPGNY is the Connecting Transmission Owner or an Affected Transmission 
9 
Owner. The CRA proposed in this filing addresses LSPGNY as the Connecting 
10 
Transmission Owner. Arrangements for LSPGNY as an Affected Transmission Owner 
11 
remain to be resolved. 
12 
The local planning provisions present a separate question. Attachment Y calls for 
13 
Transmission Owners to plan their systems, while the definitions of the Local Transmission 
14 
Owner Plan and the Local Transmission Owner Planning Process refer to the owner’s 
15 
Transmission District. Because LSPGNY has no obligation to serve load in a Transmission 
16 
District, OATT revisions are necessary to clarify how LSPGNY can plan upgrades to its 
17 
own facilities on a comparable basis. See NYISO OATT §§ 1.20, 31.1.1, and 31.2.1. 
18 
IV. NYISO STAKEHOLDER PROCESS 
19 
Q. 
HOW DID LSPGNY ENGAGE WITH NYISO? 
20 
A. 
LSPGNY discussed load study procedures with NYISO staff in late 2025 and participated 
21 
in NYISO’s discussions with Transmission Owners after the Show Cause Order. In July 
22 
2026, LSPGNY submitted questions and met with NYISO staff. In written comments on 
23

6 
NYISO’s July 23 stakeholder presentation, submitted July 27, LSPGNY requested 
1 
additional time for stakeholder review, urged a coordinated filing, and asked NYISO to 
2 
address how a Transmission Owner without retail load would participate as a Connecting 
3 
or Affected Transmission Owner. 
4 
NYISO and the incumbent Transmission Owners each filed a motion for abeyance on 
5 
August 3. LSPGNY and New York Transmission Co., LLC jointly filed a separate motion 
6 
that day. The Commission granted the motions on August 14. See Order Granting 
7 
Abeyance at PP 2, 8, 10. 
8 
On September 24, LSPGNY presented its proposed cost recovery framework to NYISO 
9 
staff and counsel. On October 8, NYISO explained that Transmission Owners should lead 
10 
the development of cost recovery frameworks and identified implementation work 
11 
involving rate design, facility treatment, billing, revenue tracking, and collateral that would 
12 
need to be addressed. LSPGNY therefore proposed including the core cost-responsibility 
13 
terms in the initial filing and addressing billing and collateral mechanics later. 
14 
Q. 
HOW DID LSPGNY COORDINATE WITH THE OTHER TRANSMISSION 
15 
OWNERS AND STAKEHOLDERS? 
16 
A. 
On July 20, 2026, LSPGNY contacted counsel for the New York Transmission Owners 
17 
(“NYTOs”) to discuss coordinating their responses to the Show Cause Order. In a follow-
18 
up discussion on July 22, LSPGNY asked to participate in developing the NYTOs’ 
19 
response and to join their filing. The NYTOs declined both requests. 
20 
 
LSPGNY continued to participate in NYISO’s Transmission Owner working sessions. It 
21 
raised two issues for an Affected Transmission Owner with no retail relationship with the 
22

7 
large load: how that owner would recover the costs of upgrades to its facilities and how it 
1 
would gain access to the financial security supporting payment of those costs. 
2 
 
On October 22, the NYTOs presented a proposed cost recovery and security framework 
3 
that relied on Section 5 of the NYISO OATT, which governs the collection of transmission 
4 
charges under participating Transmission Owners’ retail access tariffs. LSPGNY does not 
5 
serve retail customers. As a result, the proposal provided no mechanism for LSPGNY to 
6 
recover the costs of upgrades to its facilities needed to serve a large load that takes retail 
7 
service from another Transmission Owner. 
 
8 
Q. 
HOW DID THE STAKEHOLDER PROCESS AFFECT LSPGNY’S APPROACH? 
9 
A. 
The discussions identified the need for a rate provision that works for non-incumbent 
10 
Transmission Owners and for NYISO settlement rules that put that provision into effect. 
11 
The coordinated process did not yield a joint proposal that resolved both issues for 
12 
LSPGNY within the time available. LSPGNY is therefore presenting a separate framework 
13 
for upgrades where it is the Connecting Transmission Owner. Affected-system cost 
14 
recovery and security arrangements remain to be addressed in coordination with the other 
15 
Transmission Owners’ proposals and, if necessary, through a subsequent filing. It is 
16 
designed to work alongside NYISO’s regional study and interconnection procedures and 
17 
the cost recovery arrangements developed for owners with a TSC. 
18 
V. COST RECOVERY AGREEMENT 
19 
Q. 
WHO WOULD ENTER INTO THE CRA, AND WHAT WOULD IT COVER? 
20 
A. 
LSPGNY proposes a pro forma CRA between LSPGNY and the Eligible Customer taking 
21 
wholesale transmission service on behalf of the large load where LSPGNY is the 
22 
Connecting Transmission Owner. The Large Load Customer would execute a Limited 
23

8 
Acknowledgment without becoming a party to the CRA’s wholesale payment obligations. 
1 
NYISO would not be a CRA party; its billing, collection, security, draw, and remittance 
2 
responsibilities arise under the proposed Rate Schedule 10 Large Load Provisions. The 
3 
CRA identifies each Covered Upgrade, the assigned responsibility, calculation inputs, and 
4 
payment and security obligations. A Covered Upgrade includes an identified Large Load-
5 
Driven Upgrade or LSPGNY-owned ISO-Assigned Regional Project share for which the 
6 
CRA establishes an Annual MTRC. Retail arrangements between the Eligible Customer 
7 
and the Large Load Customer would remain governed by the applicable retail framework. 
8 
Q. 
WHEN WILL THE CRA AND ASSOCIATED SECURITY BE IN PLACE? 
9 
A. 
The study results would identify the Covered Upgrades and the responsibility to be 
10 
documented in the CRA and applicable construction or interconnection arrangements. 
11 
Execution or authorized effectiveness of those arrangements, and delivery of the required 
12 
construction security, will precede the construction commitments they secure. Operational 
13 
security will support the remaining revenue commitment after the applicable upgrade enters 
14 
service. The CRA establishes the applicable deadlines, conditions for proceeding, and 
15 
remedies if the Eligible Customer fails to execute the required arrangements, post security, 
16 
or maintain it. Those requirements protect against LSPGNY incurring an unsecured 
17 
obligation in reliance on the large load. 
18 
Q. 
HOW WOULD THE FRAMEWORK APPLY WHEN THE LARGE LOAD 
19 
CONNECTS TO ANOTHER TRANSMISSION OWNER’S SYSTEM? 
20 
A. 
A large load connecting to another Transmission Owner’s system may require an upgrade 
21 
to an LSPGNY facility. The applicable study would identify the required upgrade and the 
22 
responsibility attributable to the request. The proposed CRA in this filing, however, covers 
23

9 
LSPGNY as the Connecting Transmission Owner; it does not establish a CRA for 
1 
LSPGNY as an Affected Transmission Owner. The appropriate arrangement will depend 
2 
on the scope of the other Transmission Owners’ proposed agreements and the associated 
3 
tariff provisions. 
4 
 
LSPGNY needs a mechanism to recover its affected-system upgrade costs and obtain 
5 
access to the supporting security without a retail service relationship with the end-use load. 
6 
If the other Transmission Owners’ proposed agreements do not provide that mechanism, a 
7 
separate affected-system CRA may need to be added as another appendix to Attachment 1 
8 
of Rate Schedule 10 through a subsequent filing. This filing should not be understood as 
9 
resolving that remaining issue. 
10 
Q. 
HOW WOULD LSPGNY ASSIGN AND RECOVER THE COST OF A LARGE 
11 
LOAD-DRIVEN UPGRADE? 
12 
A. 
The applicable study would identify the upgrades needed to serve the requested load and 
13 
the costs attributable to that request. The CRA documents the Eligible Customer’s 
14 
responsibility for the applicable Covered Upgrades, including assigned shares where 
15 
multiple requests contribute to the need for an upgrade. That contractual responsibility is 
16 
distinct from the allocation of LSPGNY’s formula-rate revenue requirement under Rate 
17 
Schedule 10. Under LSPGNY’s proposed approach, the revenue requirements for Large 
18 
Load-Driven Upgrades would be combined with Segment A’s revenue requirement in a 
19 
single RTFC and allocated using Segment A’s existing tariff cost allocation. There would 
20 
be no separate zonal or subzonal allocation for an individual Large Load-Driven Upgrade. 
21 
Supplemental MTRC and Annual Termination Fee Remittances would reduce the 
22 
combined revenue requirement as general revenue credits under the formula rate template. 
23

10 
The costs and those credits would therefore be reflected in the same RTFC using the same 
1 
allocation. 
2 
 
The existing RTFC allocation is the established mechanism for collecting LSPGNY’s 
3 
Commission-authorized revenue requirement. Its use does not rest on a finding that the 
4 
Responsible LSEs caused the Large Load Facility or its service request. The CRA 
5 
separately assigns the responsible Eligible Customer an Annual MTRC, satisfied through 
6 
Qualifying Transmission Revenues and Supplemental MTRC. The formula rate credits the 
7 
applicable Large Load CRA Revenue against LSPGNY’s revenue requirement. These 
8 
provisions are intended to mitigate cost shifting to other Responsible LSEs, subject to the 
9 
relationship between the contractual commitment and actual cost of service described 
10 
below. 
11 
 
Where more than one Large Load Facility drives an upgrade, Schedule 1 identifies an 
12 
Initial Allocation Percentage for each Large Load Customer using the applicable final study 
13 
and allocation methodology. That allocation accounts for individually and jointly studied 
14 
loads; their requested service levels, development phases, and facility configurations; and 
15 
any portion serving other system needs or customers. Aggregate allocations to Large Load 
16 
Customers may not exceed one hundred percent. Any unallocated portion remains subject 
17 
to the otherwise applicable Rate Schedule 10 cost-allocation and recovery rules.  
18 
LSPGNY would calculate the annual cost of service through its formula rate, including 
19 
return on net rate base, depreciation, taxes, and allocable operating and administrative 
20 
expenses, subject to applicable credits. NYISO would recover the resulting revenue 
21 
requirement through Rate Schedule 10 and separately bill the Eligible Customer for 
22 
Supplemental MTRC under the CRA. LSPGNY proposes to retain the requirement for 
23

11 
Commission acceptance of a section 205 filing adding each Large Load-Driven Upgrade to 
1 
Table 1 before its revenue requirement could be included in the RTFC. Listing an upgrade 
2 
would identify the investment eligible for recovery; it would not establish a separate cost 
3 
allocation for that upgrade. LSPGNY’s recovery would be determined under its formula 
4 
rate, including the credits for CRA revenue. The Annual Update would credit Supplemental 
5 
MTRC actually received, including applicable Security proceeds received and applied to 
6 
that obligation, rather than amounts merely billed. An amount not collected or satisfied 
7 
from Security would not reduce LSPGNY’s actual formula-rate revenue requirement as a 
8 
revenue credit. The resulting difference from the projected credit would be reflected in the 
9 
ordinary formula-rate true-up and included in the next Annual Projection prepared after the 
10 
Annual Update, with ordinary true-up interest. The Eligible Customer would remain liable, 
11 
and any later recovery would be credited when received. Other transmission customers 
12 
could therefore bear a collection shortfall through the RTFC pending a later recovery; the 
13 
CRA’s payment and security obligations mitigate that exposure but do not eliminate it. 
14 
Commission acceptance of each Table 1 designation provides an opportunity to evaluate 
15 
the particular upgrade, its supporting study record, and the application of the CRA 
16 
protections before its revenue requirement enters the RTFC. 
17 
The CRA does not determine whether a facility is directly assigned or included in rate base. 
18 
That determination is made under the applicable NYISO tariff, study process, and 
19 
interconnection arrangements. Direct Assignment Facilities and other facilities whose costs 
20 
are directly assigned to and paid by the Eligible Customer, and are not included in 
21 
LSPGNY’s rate base, are excluded from the definition of Large Load-Driven Upgrades and 
22

12 
the MTRC framework. See the CRA definition of “Large Load-Driven Upgrades” and 
1 
Section 6.2. 
2 
Covered Upgrades are separately identified in the formula rate and use the capital structure 
3 
and generally applicable return components applicable to LSPGNY under Rate Schedule 
4 
10, including any Commission-approved generally applicable ROE incentive, as applicable. 
5 
They do not receive incentives specific to the AC Transmission Project or become subject 
6 
to that project’s Competitive Bid Concession, cost cap, or other project-specific cost-
7 
containment commitments. See CRA Section 6.2 and Eric Arzola’s rate testimony. 
8 
Q. 
HOW WOULD THE MINIMUM CONTRIBUTION WORK? 
9 
A. 
The CRA establishes an Annual Minimum Transmission Revenue Contribution (“Annual 
10 
MTRC”) for each Covered Upgrade using the separate MTRC Calculation Template in 
11 
Schedule 5. The calculation uses a levelized fixed charge rate (“FCR”) over a twenty-year 
12 
MTRC Term, applied to the assigned capital cost, with the capital recovery, income-tax, 
13 
and other capital-related components specified in Schedule 5, plus any fixed annual 
14 
components not included in the FCR. The calculation excludes the Segment A project-risk 
15 
incentive adder. Estimated capital cost would initially support an Estimated Annual MTRC. 
16 
LSPGNY would establish the Final Annual MTRC using actual capital cost within one year 
17 
after the Covered Upgrade enters service, with estimated charges reconciled under the 
18 
CRA. The finalized contractual MTRC would not be reset through routine annual formula-
19 
rate updates, subject to the CRA’s expressly permitted adjustments. 
20 
Q. 
WHY DOES LSPGNY PROPOSE A TWENTY-YEAR, LEVELIZED MTRC? 
21 
A. 
A large-load request may require a substantial transmission investment before the load 
22 
reaches its expected operating level. A twenty-year commitment provides an extended 
23

13 
period of customer accountability for that investment, while establishing a defined period 
1 
over which the Eligible Customer can evaluate its obligation. Levelization spreads the 
2 
calculated revenue contribution over that period rather than concentrating it in the initial 
3 
years. The purpose is to secure a meaningful contribution toward the investment 
4 
undertaken for the requested service and reduce the exposure of other customers if the load 
5 
is delayed, reduced, or discontinued. 
6 
 
The twenty-year MTRC Term is a contractual revenue-support period. Under CRA 
7 
Sections 3.2 and 6.7, earlier Break-Even is available if a final Reconciliation Statement 
8 
determines that the Total Required Revenue Commitment has been satisfied before the end 
9 
of that term. Operational payment and security obligations then terminate, subject to final 
10 
true-ups and correction of errors or fraud for periods before satisfaction. Once finally 
11 
satisfied, the responsibility does not revive because of a later change in return on equity, 
12 
expense, load, forecast, or other formula-rate input. It does not establish the upgrade’s 
13 
accounting depreciation rate or require removal of the facility from rate base at the end of 
14 
that term. The facility’s continued inclusion in the formula rate would remain governed by 
15 
the applicable tariff and Commission requirements. Amounts recovered under the CRA 
16 
would receive the credits and other treatment provided in the formula rate template so that 
17 
the contractual commitment does not create duplicate recovery. 
18 
 
The twenty-year term is supported by Operational Security based on the remaining 
19 
Cumulative Revenue Responsibility and, when the applicable termination provisions are 
20 
triggered, a Termination Fee equal to the remaining contractual commitment less any 
21 
Supplemental MTRC already billed and remaining unpaid. Those unpaid bills remain 
22 
separately payable and are not discharged by payment of the Termination Fee. It does not 
23

14 
eliminate all risk over the Covered Upgrade’s depreciable life. Neither a levelized Annual 
1 
MTRC nor the single-year illustration below, standing alone, demonstrates that the total 
2 
commitment equals or exceeds the upgrade’s cost of service over its entire life. Such a 
3 
conclusion would require a comparison using consistent cost, revenue, timing, and 
4 
discount-rate assumptions. 
5 
Q. 
WHY CAN THE FIXED ANNUAL MTRC DIFFER FROM THE UPGRADE’S 
6 
ANNUAL FORMULA-RATE REVENUE REQUIREMENT? 
7 
A. 
The Annual MTRC is a levelized contractual amount calculated using the inputs specified 
8 
in the CRA. The formula rate separately determines the annual cost of service using the 
9 
applicable rate base, depreciation, expenses, taxes, return, and credits. As net plant declines 
10 
and other formula-rate inputs change, the annual cost of service can differ from the fixed 
11 
contractual amount. The Annual MTRC is therefore not a representation that the 
12 
customer’s minimum contribution will equal the actual incremental revenue requirement in 
13 
every year. 
14 
 
The effect on other customers depends on the actual revenue requirement, qualifying large-
15 
load revenues, Supplemental MTRC, and the credit and allocation provisions in the 
16 
template and tariff. The contractual floor, security, and reconciliation provisions mitigate 
17 
exposure to the large load; they do not support an unconditional assurance that every other 
18 
customer’s rate will remain unchanged under every operating or cost scenario. 
19 
Q. 
WHY DOES THE FIXED CHARGE CALCULATION INCLUDE CAPITAL 
20 
RECOVERY, INCOME TAXES, AND OTHER SPECIFIED COMPONENTS? 
21 
A. 
Capital cost alone does not measure the full revenue contribution associated with an 
22 
upgrade. Schedule 5 calculates the Annual MTRC using a levelized capital charge rate plus 
23

15 
an expense allocator, consistent with the FCR worksheet in Exhibit No. GNY-101. The 
1 
calculation first determines an after-tax discount rate using the applicable capital structure, 
2 
return on equity, cost of debt, and composite income-tax rate. It then subtracts the present 
3 
value of federal and state tax-depreciation benefits from allocated capital cost and applies 
4 
an income-tax revenue conversion factor. The resulting present-value capital revenue 
5 
requirement is annualized over the twenty-year MTRC Term using the after-tax discount 
6 
rate and divided by allocated capital cost to determine the levelized capital charge rate. The 
7 
expense allocator reflects operating and maintenance expense, less project-specific 
8 
regulatory asset amortization included in that expense, plus taxes other than income taxes, 
9 
divided by total gross transmission plant in service. The levelized capital charge rate and 
10 
expense allocator are each rounded to six decimal places and added to determine the Fixed 
11 
Charge Rate. The Annual MTRC equals allocated capital cost multiplied by that rate, plus 
12 
any separately identified fixed annual costs not already included. Supporting workpapers 
13 
identify the inputs, their sources, and each calculation, and prevent duplicate inclusion of 
14 
any cost. 
15 
 
The FCR calculation establishes the contractual minimum contribution; it is not an 
16 
additional formula-rate charge imposed on top of the same cost of service without an offset. 
17 
LSPGNY would continue to calculate its revenue requirement through the formula rate, 
18 
and Supplemental MTRC and other applicable amounts would receive the treatment 
19 
specified in the template. Schedule 5 and its supporting workpapers provide the contractual 
20 
calculation and input reconciliation; the separate rate testimony of Eric Arzola explains 
21 
how the resulting Annual MTRC is used in the formula rate template. 
22

16 
The MTRC is a contractual revenue floor calculated separately from LSPGNY’s annual 
1 
formula-rate cost of service. Supplemental MTRC is the greater of zero and the applicable 
2 
Annual MTRC less Qualifying Transmission Revenues for the corresponding period. The 
3 
CRA and Schedule 2 define the qualifying RTFC revenues attributable to the Large Load 
4 
Facility and the methodology for attributing or allocating those revenues among Covered 
5 
Upgrades. Each dollar would count only once. LSPGNY would maintain customer- and 
6 
Covered Upgrade-specific records of the commitment and its satisfaction. That tracking 
7 
does not require formula-rate credits to be applied exclusively to the revenue requirement 
8 
of the corresponding upgrade. Instead, CRA revenue is a general revenue credit that 
9 
reduces LSPGNY’s overall revenue requirement rather than the revenue requirement of any 
10 
individual Covered Upgrade. 
11 
Qualifying Transmission Revenues are not a separate retail or load-based charge imposed 
12 
by LSPGNY. They are the portion of RTFC revenues assessed on the Large Load Facility’s 
13 
Actual Energy Withdrawals, collected from the Responsible LSE or LSEs serving that 
14 
facility, and remitted to LSPGNY that is attributable to the applicable Covered Upgrade 
15 
and reduces the RTFC otherwise collected from other Responsible LSEs. Schedule 2 
16 
provides the methodology using the applicable metering data, RTFC rate, Load Zone or 
17 
Subzone allocation, and Covered Upgrade Revenue Share.  
18 
Q. 
DOES THE CRA REPLACE ORDINARY TRANSMISSION-SERVICE PAYMENT 
19 
OR COLLATERAL OBLIGATIONS? 
20 
A. 
No. The Eligible Customer and the transmission customers responsible for the combined 
21 
RTFC would remain subject to their respective payment obligations under the applicable 
22 
transmission tariffs. The CRA determines which qualifying RTFC revenues attributable to 
23

17 
the Large Load Facility satisfy the minimum contribution. Supplemental MTRC would be 
1 
due only for the positive difference between the applicable Annual MTRC and those 
2 
qualifying revenues. It would not replace ordinary transmission charges or permit the same 
3 
revenue to be credited twice.

CRA security supports the obligations established by that agreement. Ordinary 
5 
transmission-service credit requirements continue to apply under the governing tariff.

Qualifying retail security support may satisfy the corresponding CRA security exposure

only to the extent the CRA and tariff recognize it and the support is legally available when 
8 
needed.

Q. 
HOW WOULD PROJECTED AND ACTUAL AMOUNTS BE RECONCILED? 
10 
A. 
LSPGNY would include the projected Supplemental MTRC, including any prior-period 
11 
true-up adjustment, and any projected Annual Termination Fee Remittances as a credit in 
12 
the Annual Projection in accordance with the formula rate template, and NYISO would bill 
13 
and remit the applicable customer-specific amounts under the tariff and CRA. In the 
14 
Annual Update, that projected credit would be replaced by Supplemental MTRC cash 
15 
receipts and Annual Termination Fee Remittances actually received during the Rate Year, 
16 
supported by billing, cash-receipt, and settlement records. Supplemental MTRC receipts 
17 
would include applicable Security proceeds received and applied to Supplemental MTRC 
18 
obligations and later collections of amounts billed in earlier years, counted once. 
19 
Differences between projected credits and actual receipts would flow through the ordinary 
20 
formula-rate true-up. The separate customer-level reconciliation would continue to 
21 
compare amounts billed with the contractual amount due; nonpayment would not itself 
22 
create an additional customer-level charge. The CRA Reconciliation Statement compares 
23

18 
the Supplemental MTRC billed for the Rate Year, excluding any prior-period true-up 
1 
adjustment included in that billing, with the actual Supplemental MTRC determined from 
2 
actual Qualifying Transmission Revenues. The difference, calculated without interest, 
3 
would be carried into the Eligible Customer’s projected Supplemental MTRC in the next 
4 
Annual Projection as a prior-period true-up adjustment. If no further Supplemental MTRC 
5 
will be billed under the CRA, LSPGNY would include any under-billed amount in a 
6 
Charge Statement and refund any over-billed amount to the Eligible Customer, in each case 
7 
without interest. The Reconciliation Statement would serve as a supporting worksheet 
8 
rather than impose an additional charge or duplicate a template calculation. This annual 
9 
reconciliation is separate from finalizing the MTRC using actual capital cost. An example 
10 
CRA Reconciliation Statement is provided as Exhibit No. GNY-102.

12 
ANNUAL PROJECTION? 
13 
A. 
Reflecting projected Supplemental MTRC allows the expected contribution to reduce the 
14 
amount initially recovered from other transmission customers under the template. If the 
15 
contribution were excluded until after receipt and a later true-up, those customers could 
16 
temporarily bear amounts that the CRA assigns to the Eligible Customer. The projection 
17 
uses the expected upgrade in-service dates, load, qualifying revenues, and applicable 
18 
Annual MTRC. Those assumptions are subject to reconciliation when actual information 
19 
becomes available.

22 
excluding any prior-period true-up adjustment included in that billing, and the actual 
23

19

1

2 
interest if no further Supplemental MTRC will be billed under the CRA. This approach 
3 
combines timely recognition of the expected customer contribution with correction of 
4 
forecast differences at the customer level. Collection risk is treated separately. Because the 
5 
Annual Update credits actual cash receipts, a delayed or unpaid amount not satisfied from 
6 
Security would reduce the actual revenue credit and could increase the amount recovered 
7 
from other customers through the ordinary formula-rate true-up, with applicable interest. 
8 
The unpaid amount would remain owed by the Eligible Customer and subject to the CRA’s 
9 
payment and security provisions. Any later recovery would be credited in the year received, 
10 
without duplicating a previously recognized receipt. The principal reason for projected 
11 
treatment is timely protection of other customers, supported by transparent reconciliation.

13

14 
A.

15 
requirement and a credit for the projected Supplemental MTRC and any Annual 
16 
Termination Fee Remittances for that year. By October 31 preceding Rate Year Y, 
17 
LSPGNY would deliver a Charge Statement to NYISO, and during Rate Year Y, NYISO 
18

the tariff and CRA. By June 30 of Rate Year Y+1, LSPGNY would prepare the Annual 
20 
Update using actual information for Rate Year Y, together with a Reconciliation Statement 
21 
identifying the prior-period true-up adjustment. That adjustment would be included in the 
22 
next Annual Projection and therefore billed during Rate Year Y+2, under the timetable 
23

20 
specified in the template and tariff. Separately, the Annual Update in Rate Year Y+1 would 
1 
replace the projected CRA revenue credit for Rate Year Y with actual receipts during Rate 
2 
Year Y. The resulting ordinary formula-rate true-up, including applicable interest, would be 
3 
included in the Annual Projection prepared in Y+1 for recovery or credit in Rate Year Y+2. 
4 
A later collection would be recognized as a revenue credit in the year received and 
5 
reconciled through that year’s Annual Update. Workpapers would identify the billing year 
6 
and receipt year so that a later collection is not mistaken for a new obligation or credited 
7 
twice. An example Charge Statement illustrating the billing instructions LSPGNY would 
8 
deliver to NYISO is provided as Exhibit No. GNY-103.

requirement. Interest calculated under 18 C.F.R. § 35.19a would apply to an amount 
15 
determined through a dispute to have been overbilled. The ordinary formula-rate over- or 
16 
under-recovery resulting from differences between projected Large Load CRA Revenue 
17 
and actual cash receipts, including collection shortfalls and later recoveries, would be 
18 
subject to the ordinary formula-rate true-up interest provisions. That interest would apply 
19 
through the formula-rate true-up and would not impose interest on the separate customer-
20 
level Supplemental MTRC reconciliation. The template and supporting workpapers 
21 
distinguish these types of adjustments.
